title: Innate Domain: importing a Shikigami library
description:
`Innate Domain: lib/shapes` loads examples/lib/shapes.domain before this
program, so its operations are callable by name — exactly like the prelude's.
Imports are declarations, not pipeline steps, so the line can sit anywhere;
by convention it goes at the top.

so `Biggest` fuses into a quickselect just as if it had been written here.

title: A `Using:` written as an indented pipeline instead of a lambda
description:
`All Pairs` searches the *current value*, so over a List<List<Int>> it would
pair whole rows against each other. Writing Map Each's `Using:` as a pipeline
runs that pipeline in the lambda's place, once per row with the row as its
current value — the only way to reach a primitive per element, since the
expression layer has no way to iterate. A body stands in for any 1-parameter
`Using:` lambda, not just Map Each's: `Filter`, `Sort By`, `Group By` and the
rest take one too.

Each row here holds exactly one evenly-divisible pair (AoC 2017 day 2 part
2). The body finds it and divides it; the outer pipeline sums the results.
source:
# A `Using:` written as an indented pipeline instead of a lambda.
#
# `All Pairs` searches the *current value*, so over a List<List<Int>> it would
# pair whole rows against each other. Writing Map Each's `Using:` as a pipeline
# runs that pipeline in the lambda's place, once per row with the row as its
# current value — the only way to reach a primitive per element, since the
# expression layer has no way to iterate. A body stands in for any 1-parameter
# `Using:` lambda, not just Map Each's: `Filter`, `Sort By`, `Group By` and the
# rest take one too.
#
# Each row here holds exactly one evenly-divisible pair (AoC 2017 day 2 part
# 2). The body finds it and divides it; the outer pipeline sums the results.
#
#   domain examples/19_row_pairs.domain
#   Expected output: 9
Cursed Energy: 19_row_pairs.input
Shikigami: Lines
Cursed Technique: Extract Integers
Cursed Technique: Map Each
    Domain Expansion: All Pairs
        Mode: First
        Using: (a, b) -> (a % b = 0) or (b % a = 0)
    Maximum Technique: Reduce
        Using: (x, y) -> max(x, y) / min(x, y)
Maximum Technique: Sum
Reveal: stdout

title: Local bindings: naming a value for one stage's expressions
description:
The lambda below needs the mean of the whole list, which no lambda can reach
on its own — it sees one element at a time. `Consider mean Of …` computes it
once from the value entering the stage and binds it by name for every
expression on that stage.

The preposition says where a binding's value comes from, and it has to: a
1-parameter lambda already means two different things in Domain depending on
where it is written (per element in a `Using:`, once over the current value
in a measured argument like `Size:`), and a binding has no slot to say which.
So `As` never sees the pipeline value — it binds a constant or a function —
and `Of` always does.

The two `As` bindings cost nothing at all: `tolerance` folds into the lambda
as a literal and `spread` is inlined at its call site, so both are gone
before either backend sees the program.
source:
# Local bindings: naming a value for one stage's expressions.
#
# The lambda below needs the mean of the whole list, which no lambda can reach
# on its own — it sees one element at a time. `Consider mean Of …` computes it
# once from the value entering the stage and binds it by name for every
# expression on that stage.
#
# The preposition says where a binding's value comes from, and it has to: a
# 1-parameter lambda already means two different things in Domain depending on
# where it is written (per element in a `Using:`, once over the current value
# in a measured argument like `Size:`), and a binding has no slot to say which.
# So `As` never sees the pipeline value — it binds a constant or a function —
# and `Of` always does.
#
# The two `As` bindings cost nothing at all: `tolerance` folds into the lambda
# as a literal and `spread` is inlined at its call site, so both are gone
# before either backend sees the program.
#
#   domain examples/20_stage_locals.domain
#   Expected output: 3
Cursed Energy: 20_stage_locals.input
Shikigami: Lines
Channeled Energy: Convert List to Integers
Maximum Technique: Count Matching
    Consider tolerance As 5
    Consider spread As (a, b) -> a - b
    Consider mean Of (xs) -> sum(xs) / length(xs)
    Using: (x) -> spread(x, mean) > tolerance
Reveal: stdout

title: A first-class graph: parse an edge list once, then ask it several questions
description:
Before Graph<K> an explicit graph had nowhere to live. BFS and Dijkstra took
a Grid, so they only reached geometry; Explore takes a successor lambda, so
its graph is implicit and cannot be built once and queried twice; and
Topological Sort's adjacency map had to be rebuilt at every stage and had
nowhere to put a weight. `Convert To Graph` gives the parse somewhere to go.

The roads are undirected, which is one arc each way — `Mode: Undirected` is
how you say that, rather than a second kind of value.

`Shortest Path` answers which way rather than how far: the cheapest route
from London to Exeter is via Bristol (118 + 84 = 202), not via Oxford
(57 + 74 + 84 = 215), even though both are three cities.
source:
# A first-class graph: parse an edge list once, then ask it several questions.
#
# Before Graph<K> an explicit graph had nowhere to live. BFS and Dijkstra took
# a Grid, so they only reached geometry; Explore takes a successor lambda, so
# its graph is implicit and cannot be built once and queried twice; and
# Topological Sort's adjacency map had to be rebuilt at every stage and had
# nowhere to put a weight. `Convert To Graph` gives the parse somewhere to go.
#
# The roads are undirected, which is one arc each way — `Mode: Undirected` is
# how you say that, rather than a second kind of value.
#
# `Shortest Path` answers which way rather than how far: the cheapest route
# from London to Exeter is via Bristol (118 + 84 = 202), not via Oxford
# (57 + 74 + 84 = 215), even though both are three cities.
#
#   domain examples/21_graph_routes.domain
#   Expected output: london->bristol->exeter
Cursed Energy: 21_graph_routes.input
Shikigami: Lines
Cursed Technique: Split Each by " "
Cursed Technique: Map Each
    Using: (r) -> tuple(item(r, 0), item(r, 1), toint(item(r, 2)))
Channeled Energy: Convert To Graph
    Mode: Undirected
Domain Expansion: Shortest Path
    Start: "london"
    Goal: "exeter"
Maximum Technique: Join with "->"
Reveal: stdout
input:
london bristol 118
london oxford 57
oxford bristol 74
bristol exeter 84
oxford birmingham 65
birmingham manchester 88
manchester leeds 44
leeds york 25

source:
# Maximum subarray sum (Kadane's algorithm) — the classic dynamic
# programming exercise: the largest sum of any contiguous run.
#
# The fold state is a two-element list [best, current]. The main pipeline
# holds the seed (built from the first element); the Channel carries the
# rest of the numbers for Fold From: to run over.
#
#   domain challenges/03_max_subarray.domain
Cursed Energy: 03_max_subarray.input
Shikigami: Ints

Channel "rest":
    Cursed Technique: Apply
        Using: (xs) -> drop(xs, 1)

Cursed Technique: Apply
    Using: (xs) -> list(item(xs, 0), item(xs, 0))
Maximum Technique: Fold
    From: rest
    Using: (acc, x) -> list(max(list(first(acc), max(list(x, last(acc) + x)))), max(list(x, last(acc) + x)))
Cursed Technique: Apply
    Using: (acc) -> first(acc)
Reveal: stdout

title: Conway's Game of Life — a glider on an infinite plane, run 4 generations
description:
The board is a Sparse grid, so there are no edges to clip the glider. One
generation is the classic counting trick: every live cell contributes 1
to each of its 8 neighbors and 9 to itself, so after Count By a cell's
score is neighbors + 9*alive — and the next generation is exactly the
cells scoring 3 (birth), 11, or 12 (survival). After 4 generations a
glider is itself, translated one step diagonally — which the densified
bounding-box picture normalizes away, so the output equals the input.
source:
# Conway's Game of Life — a glider on an infinite plane, run 4 generations.
#
# The board is a Sparse grid, so there are no edges to clip the glider. One
# generation is the classic counting trick: every live cell contributes 1
# to each of its 8 neighbors and 9 to itself, so after Count By a cell's
# score is neighbors + 9*alive — and the next generation is exactly the
# cells scoring 3 (birth), 11, or 12 (survival). After 4 generations a
# glider is itself, translated one step diagonally — which the densified
# bounding-box picture normalizes away, so the output equals the input.
#
#   domain challenges/11_game_of_life.domain
Cursed Energy: 11_game_of_life.input
Shikigami: Lines
Cursed Technique: Match Pattern
    Using: "{int},{int}"
    Mode: Each
Channeled Energy: Convert To Sparse Grid
    Default: 0
    Mark: 1
Simple Domain: Repeat 4
    Cursed Technique: Find Cells
        Using: (v) -> v = 1
    Cursed Technique: Map Each
        Using: (p) -> list(padd(p, point(-1, -1)), padd(p, point(-1, 0)), padd(p, point(-1, 1)), padd(p, point(0, -1)), padd(p, point(0, 1)), padd(p, point(1, -1)), padd(p, point(1, 0)), padd(p, point(1, 1)), p, p, p, p, p, p, p, p, p)
    Cursed Technique: Flatten
    Maximum Technique: Count By
        Using: (q) -> q
    Channeled Energy: Convert To Sparse Grid
        Default: 0
    Cursed Technique: Find Cells
        Using: (score) -> score = 3 or score = 11 or score = 12
    Channeled Energy: Convert To Sparse Grid
        Default: 0
        Mark: 1
Cursed Technique: Map Cells
    Using: (v) -> if v = 1 then "#" else "."
Channeled Energy: Convert To Grid
Reveal: stdout

title: Minesweeper board — given the mines, render the numbers: each cell shows
description:
how many of its 8 neighbors are mines, mines show *.

Same weighted-count trick as Game of Life: every mine adds 1 to each
neighbor and 9 to itself, so any score of 9 or more is a mine and the

untouched cells stay quiet.
